messages.subject: stat_summary(fun.y=var,geom=c("point","smooth"))
parts:
Hi,

I'm not sure if this is a feature request or a question. Is there a
way to specify multiple geoms in the same way as qplot? I'm guessing
that no because it is against the ggplot way of building up layer by
layer and this would build two layers at once; but I still think it
would be nice, but you might have a long stat_() call that is
complicated and to replicate it would be confusing to read where as
the c("point","smooth") is more readable.

So I guess 2 questions:
1. Is there a way to specify multiple geoms in ggplot besides qplot?
2. If not, is it because it goes against the layer-by-layer philosophy
or another reason?

Thanks!

Xu.

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: stat_summary(fun.y=var,geom=c("point","smooth"))
parts:
Hi:

It is common to combine multiple geoms into a single plot, but they
are applied individually in separate layers. If your question is 'can
I apply multiple geoms at once into a single layer?' then the answer
is no. A single geom, on the other hand, allows the use of multiple
aesthetics. The + operator exists to allow one to add additional
layers as needed to a ggplot. Most people who produce relatively
complicated graphics in ggplot2 eventually move to using ggplot()
rather than qplot(), but it is certainly possible to add layers to
qplot() as well using the + operator.

Here's a plot I did tonight using some baseball data; the data are not
included, but the plot code illustrates the point:

ggplot(topHitters, aes(x = yearID, y = BA)) +
geom_point(aes(colour = ba400), size = 2.5) +
geom_hline(yintercept = 0.400, size = 1) +
geom_text(data = bignames, aes(x = yearID + xoffset, y = BA + yoffset,
label = nameLast), size = 3) +
scale_colour_manual(values = c('FALSE' = 'black', 'TRUE' = 'red')) +
ylim(0.330, 0.430) +
xlab('Year') +
scale_y_continuous('Batting average',
breaks = seq(0.34, 0.42, by = 0.02),
labels = c('.340', '.360', '.380', '.400', '.420')) +
geom_smooth() +
opts(legend.position = 'none')

This plot contains points in a scatterplot, a horizontal reference
line, some text labels, separate colors for the points above and below
the reference line (indicated by a factor ba400 created in the data)
plus a means of assigning colors with the scale_manual() construct. I
then restrict the range of the y-axis, label the x-axis, fix labels
for the y-axis so that I get three decimal places rather than the
default two, add a loess curve to illustrate the trend over time and
finally, get rid of the legend. The plot is meant to resemble one that
appeared in the New York Times the Sunday before last (the loess curve
is graphical sugar :). There are five layers, three scale adjustments
and one line of code to remove the legend. Note that items within an
aes() statement are variables, while those outside aes() are set to a
constant value.

If this is new to you, the arguments to ggplot() are firstly, the data
frame, and secondly, the primary aesthetics that are intended to
persist in all layers of the plot (here, year and average, the x and y
variables). Notice that in geom_text(), another data frame was used,
containing labels and positional offsets to avoid overlapping of
labels in the final plot.

If you want to create 'template' plots for certain applications, you
can always write a function (or collection of functions) to produce
them; that's one way to approach what you seem to have in mind.
Another option, if you're more inclined toward interactive
construction of plots, is to look into the Deducer package, which is,
roughly speaking, a type of GUI for R with support for ggplot2 that
gives you the ability to create your own geoms from existing ones. It
uses the JGR package, which in turn requires the rJava package as its
engine. See the Deducer package home page for more details if you're
interested.
http://www.deducer.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php?n=Main.DeducerManual

Hope this is at least close to answering your question...
Dennis

parts:
Dear Dennis,

Again, thank you for your insightful and detailed reply. I appreciate
your help! I think I like your recommendation of looking into creating
template plots. I will experiment with that. I was originally
interested in this because sometimes I have a very long
stat_something(.......................) and instead of having to have
two of those long things if I wanted two geoms, I could have just
specified two geoms within just one of those long things.

Thank you,

Xu
